title: Is This a $3,000 Mistake? Gold vs Singapore Stocks
article:
Holding a physical gold bar worth $3,000 feels solid and reassuring.
You can hold it in your hand, feel its weight, and lock it away safely in a vault.
By contrast, paper shares in the stock market can feel intangible and uncertain.
So, is buying gold actually the safer choice for your hard-earned capital?
The Problem with Non-Productive Assets
Whether gold turns out to be a
good investment
depends almost entirely on when you buy it.
If you bought gold when it was trading at US$3,500 an ounce and watched it rise to US$4,500, you would feel like a genius.
But if you bought at a peak of US$5,500 an ounce, you would be staring at a US$1,000 loss per ounce.
Beyond price fluctuations, physical gold suffers from one fatal limitation: it does nothing.
Gold does not grow in size.
It does not generate profits, and it does not pay you an income.
A one-ounce gold bar locked in a safe deposit box will still be the exact same one-ounce bar in 10 or 20 years’ time.
Gold is fine as a memento to pass down to future generations, but as a long-term wealth generator, it relies entirely on finding someone else willing to pay a higher price for it down the road.
People often flock to gold during
geopolitical panics
as a supposed safe haven, but holding a piece of metal does not make world events any more certain.
Why Productive Assets Build True Wealth
To build sustainable wealth, you need to invest in productive assets.
Across the financial landscape, there are four main asset classes: cash in the bank, bonds, real estate, and equities.
Unlike gold, productive assets generate ongoing cash flow:
Cash:
Pays a basic bank interest rate.
Bonds:
Pay a fixed coupon yield.
Property:
Generates regular rental income.
Shares:
Distribute a portion of corporate profits directly to you as dividend yield.
When you invest in quality Singapore businesses, you are buying a piece of a profit-generating entity.
These companies operate in the real economy, serve customers daily, and return their earnings to shareholders through
dividends
.
While gold prices move up and down based on market fear, well-managed, cash-generative businesses work constantly to expand their operations.
Pick the right companies, and you will be rewarded with steady, increasing dividend checks over time.
Get Smart: Conviction Beats Market Volatility
Gold may offer temporary comfort during market panics, but non-productive assets cannot match the long-term wealth creation of cash-generative businesses.
By anchoring your portfolio in productive, income-paying stocks, you build a self-sustaining cash flow engine that works for you through every market cycle.

title: Smart Look At The Week Ahead: Singtel, Starhub, Sea Limited, Cisco and CoreWeave
article:
There are no significant central bank interest-rate decisions pencilled in for the week. But there is no shortage of Federal Reserve governors that are expected to take to the rostrum. It should keep the market guessing about which monetary path the US central bank will take, following the surprising mid-term elections.
On tap are speeches from Michelle Bowman, Austan Goolsbee, Tom Barkin, Chris Waller, Lorie Logan, Jeffrey Schmid, Beth Hammack, Michael Barr, Mary Daly, John Wliiams, Philip Jefferson. Some are known to be hawks, whilst some believe that interest rates should be cut.
What is undeniable is that both the core inflation rate and the headline inflation rate remain above the Fed’s target of 2%. Another set of bad inflation numbers on Tuesday could make it difficult for the Federal Open Market Committee to ignore that prices in the US are showing no signs of abating,
On the corporate front
As the earnings season winds down in the US, attention now turns to Asia. But there are still a few stragglers that are expected to take to the spotlight in America.
Cisco Systems
(Nasdaq: CSCO) is scheduled to report first-quarter numbers. The network-gear maker is expected to benefit from the continuing build out of AI infrastructure by hyperscalers. It could post a sequential rise in both quarterly earnings and revenue.
Applied Materials
(NYSE: AMAT) makes the chip-making equipment that allows chip makers to make chips. Its machines have been in demand as the rollout of AI has fuelled demand for its machinery. The company could post another set of strong fourth-quarter numbers, with revenue and earnings up strongly.
Another AI-related company is pencilled in for quarterly results.
CoreWeave
(Nasdaq: CRWV) rents out its specialised infrastructure to developers to train AI models. The neocloud outfit could report a sharp rise in revenue and a reversal of a second-quarter loss into a profit for the third quarter.
Sea Limited
(NYSE: SE), which owns the internet shopping website, Shopee, reaffirmed its outlook for the full when it reported second-quarter numbers in August. For the third quarter, the gaming and e-tailer company could post a significant rise on earnings per share in revenue of around US$8 billion.
Turning to local issue, Singapore’s two dominant telecom companies are expected to report half-year numbers. In August,
Singtel
(SGX: Z74) reported a 21% rise in first-quarter underlying profit thanks to strong contributions from regional associates Airtel and AIS. More of the same is on the cards when the telecom company reports halftime figures.
Meanwhile,
StarHub
(SGX: CC3) will provide a third-quarter business update. In October, Singapore’s second-largest telco said it will buy MyRepublic’s mobile business. It appears that consolidation is happening in Singapore. Starhub has said that there is a natural progression in which mobile virtual network operators (VMNO) will gravitate around and then be absorbed and adopted by the large, well-capitalised players. Could it have its eyes on another player?

title: OCBC Beats Expectations While DBS and UOB Miss: What Happened in 3Q 2026?
article:
If you own shares in
Singapore’s local banks
, last week was a busy one.
United Overseas Bank Limited
(SGX: U11), or UOB, reported last Wednesday, 4 November 2026, followed by
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) on Thursday.
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, wrapped things up on Friday morning.
Only OCBC delivered a profit above analysts’ estimates for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026).
Before you read too much into that, remember that a “beat” or a “miss” only compares a bank’s results with a forecast.
It doesn’t tell you whether the business is getting stronger or weaker.
For that, you need to dig deeper.
OCBC: How did a bank with lower income beat forecasts?
OCBC’s net profit rose 3.2% year on year (YoY) to S$2.04 billion, just above the S$2.01 billion average estimate from four analysts polled by LSEG.
In other words, the beat was a narrow one, at about 1.5%.
Total income slipped 1.7% YoY to S$3.73 billion.
Insurance income fell 37% to S$198 million as
Great Eastern Holdings Limited
(SGX: G07) booked mark-to-market losses on its bond portfolio.
Look past the insurance arm, and you’ll find a bank in good shape.
OCBC’s banking operations posted a record net profit of S$1.90 billion, up 16% YoY.
Customer loans grew 14% in constant-currency terms to S$372 billion, which lifted net interest income (NII) by 3.9% to S$2.3 billion.
That’s despite a net interest margin (NIM) that narrowed to 1.66% from 1.84%.
Trading income dipped 10.2% to S$465 million, the mildest decline among the three banks.
If you’re waiting for a
dividend
, it’s not due yet.
OCBC pays dividends only at its half-year and full-year results.
Management has raised its 2026 guidance to low-double-digit loan growth and kept its 50% dividend payout ratio.
DBS: Why did a growing bank miss forecasts?
DBS’s net profit fell 4.8% YoY to S$2.81 billion, short of the S$2.90 billion LSEG consensus.
The main culprit was markets trading income, which fell 65% YoY to S$152 million amid unfavourable equity market conditions.
Set that aside, and the core business kept growing.
Customer loans rose 9.5% to S$478.6 billion.
NII climbed 3.7% to S$3.71 billion even though NIM narrowed to 1.87% from 1.96%.
Net fee and commission income grew 6% to S$1.43 billion.
If you own DBS, you have a dividend coming, as it is the only local bank that pays one every quarter.
The bank declared an ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share, 10% higher than the S$0.60 paid a year ago.
On top of that, you’ll receive a capital return dividend of S$0.15 per share, unchanged from a year ago.
UOB: Why did profit more than double yet still miss?
UOB’s net profit rose 182.2% YoY to S$1.25 billion.
Don’t let that number fool you.
A year ago, UOB set aside S$1.36 billion in allowances, which shrank its 3Q2025 profit to S$443 million.
Against forecasts, UOB missed by the widest margin.
Profit came in about 7.4% below the S$1.35 billion LSEG estimate.
Trading and investment income fell 33% YoY to S$322 million.
UOB’s NIM also narrowed to 1.68%, down 6 basis points from the previous quarter as funding costs rose.
Management now expects full-year NIM below 1.75%, down from its earlier guidance of 1.75% to 1.80%.
On the flip side, UOB’s fee business hit a record.
Net fee income rose 19% to S$733 million, with wealth management fees reaching a record S$258 million.
The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio eased to 1.5% from 1.6%.
Like OCBC, UOB pays dividends twice a year, so no dividend was due this quarter.
What do the three results tell you?
Trading income fell at all three banks.
UOB also faced a shrinking margin.
Here’s the thing: the parts of each bank that fund your dividends kept growing.
All three banks grew their loans and NII YoY.
All three also lowered their NPL ratios.
Get Smart: Look past the scorecard
When a bank misses forecasts, it’s tempting to treat it as bad news.
But a forecast is a guess about a single quarter.
Your dividends depend on years of lending and fee income.
So the next time a bank misses, ask yourself one question: did the miss come from trading, or from the core business?
Trading income rises and falls with the markets.
A shrinking loan book or a rise in bad loans is a far bigger warning sign for your dividends.
This quarter, all three banks passed that test.
The number to keep an eye on next is NIM.
OCBC expects
higher US interest rates
to lift its NII as its assets reprice, while UOB has just cut its margin guidance.
How each bank handles interest rates in 2027 will shape how much your dividends can grow.

That shareholder is Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore.
It owns 50.6% of Singtel and 50.6% of SIA, both as of 2 June 2026.
It also holds a deemed interest of 40.3% in SATS as of 19 May 2026.
What they don’t share is the same set of pressures.
For context, all three last reported on the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (1QFY2027), which ended on 30 June 2026.
Two of the three felt the strain of Middle East tensions.
Can Singtel keep beating its own guidance?
Singtel
got off to a fast start.
Operating profit rose 10% year on year (YoY) to S$462 million in 1QFY2027.
That’s ahead of management’s guidance for low- to mid-single-digit growth for the full year.
Underlying net profit climbed 21% to S$831 million.
So where did the growth come from? Singtel’s growth engines.
IT services arm NCS grew operating profit 29% YoY to S$102 million on better delivery margins.
Optus added 14% to A$152 million on stronger mobile performance.
Back home, Singtel Singapore’s operating profit slipped 2% to S$230 million amid intense price competition.
Revenue grew 5% to S$3.6 billion, though, on a constant-currency basis, it was flat.
In other words, currency movements drove the top-line growth.
On 13 November, check first whether operating profit is still running ahead of guidance.
Then check whether the decline in Singapore has levelled off.
Keep an eye on capital management, too.
Singtel has raised around S$6.8 billion of its S$9 billion asset-recycling target and has used 41% of its S$2 billion buyback.
Up to S$3.3 billion in value realisation dividends is still to come through to FY2030.
Remember, Singtel pays dividends only at the half-year and full-year marks.
Will SATS turn profit growth into cash?
SATS grew its business, but its cash didn’t follow.
Revenue rose 11.3% YoY to S$1.7 billion in 1QFY2027 on new client wins and shifting trade flows.
Net profit increased 6% to S$75.1 million.
Here’s the thing: free cash flow came in at negative S$22.6 million.
Operating cash flow after lease repayment fell to S$23.2 million from S$45.8 million a year ago.
SATS blamed the timing of working capital.
On 11 November, look for signs of a recovery.
Margins are the next thing to watch.
Operating margin narrowed to 8.0% from 8.3% a year ago.
Middle East disruptions to cargo flows and inflationary pressure weighed on margins.
Management has also cautioned that inflationary pressures could add to costs in the coming quarter, and that the Middle East situation is weighing on aviation demand.
SATS carried S$4.2 billion of total debt as at 30 June 2026.
Gross debt to equity held steady at 1.41 times.
It held S$726.0 million in cash, which puts net debt, including leases, at about S$3.5 billion.
SATS declared no dividend in 1Q, the same as a year ago.
Can SIA’s fares keep pace with fuel?
SIA’s 1QFY2027 business update showed record revenue of S$5.7 billion, up 19.3% YoY.
The group still swung to a net loss of S$75.8 million, from a profit of S$186.1 million a year ago.
How does an airline lose money on record revenue? Fuel.
Net fuel expenses rose 78.5%, or S$991 million, as
jet fuel prices
spiked on the back of the Middle East conflict.
SIA’s share of Air India’s wider losses added to the pressure.
SIA did push back with higher prices.
Passenger yields improved 12% YoY, and cargo yields rose 28.1%.
Management flagged, though, that fare adjustments cannot fully offset higher fuel prices.
So on 11 November, the key question is whether higher yields can narrow the gap.
On the flip side, SIA’s cash flow tells a happier story than its profit; the airline generated about S$810 million of free cash flow.
As at 30 June 2026, it held S$9.1 billion in cash and bank balances against total debt of S$10.7 billion.
SIA pays dividends only at its half-year and full-year results.
If you own the shares for income, watch which one any dividend decision tracks: the profit or the cash.
Get Smart: Check the cash before the profit
SATS grew its profit in 1Q but burned cash.
SIA booked a loss but generated about S$810 million of free cash flow.
Profit and cash don’t always move together.
So when these results land, start with the cash flow statement.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, after all.
Then ask yourself whether the profit story and the cash story agree.
If they don’t, find out which one management expects to change.

title: Coinbase gets final regulatory stamp for trust-bank charter
article:
(Nov 9): Coinbase Global Inc, the largest US crypto exchange, said a key regulator has fully signed off on its request to become a nationally chartered trust bank, the latest example of firms in the digital-asset space entering the world of traditional finance.

The licence, approved last week by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), will help Coinbase grow its custody business and move deeper into areas such as payments, according to its application. It could also expand the company’s stablecoin business by allowing Coinbase to issue its own stablecoins and help other crypto firms with issuing and managing those tokens, according to people familiar with the matter.

A wave of digital-asset companies have applied for national trust charters and many have received preliminary approval from the OCC during President Donald Trump’s second term. Only a handful have passed the finish line, including Coinbase, Circle Internet Group Inc and Ripple.

While a trust charter is more limited than a full bank charter, it does weave these OCC-regulated institutions into the infrastructure of Wall Street. Trust banks can’t take ordinary deposits or make loans the way regular lenders do, but they handle other fiduciary and custody services that are core to the financial system.

“Our approval shows that crypto is here to stay and we are building the institutions to match,” Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, said in an interview. “And it shows we are more connected to our federal regulatory infrastructure, something we’ve long championed. That’s precisely how crypto gets integrated into our financial system.”

The OCC did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.

See also: Binance’s CFO leaves company in wake of US$6 bil crypto heist

Coinbase is already the world’s biggest crypto custodian, according to chief executive Brian Armstrong. Even before receiving the OCC charter, it’s been expanding its presence in payments and stablecoins, which are cryptocurrencies that mimic other assets including the US dollar.

The company recently partnered with Citigroup Inc for fiat-to-stablecoin conversions. It then teamed up with Ripple last month to bring that company’s stablecoin to Coinbase’s platforms. Coinbase also shares revenue with Circle for its USDC token, the second-largest stablecoin in circulation.

The OCC had granted Coinbase conditional approval for its charter in April. Coinbase was previously regulated on state level.

title: European Investment Bank’s Calvino says US turmoil is driving capital to Europe
article:
(Nov 9): Europe is set to benefit from recent market turmoil in the US as investors seek a safe haven, according to European Investment Bank (EIB) president Nadia Calvino.

“Turbulence in the US is making capital flow to Europe,” she told Bloomberg TV in an interview on Monday. “I expect that to continue.”

Calvino said she doesn’t see any negative impact on investment in Europe at the moment, adding that there had been very strong demand for EIB bond issuance and that she expects more of the same in January.

“Right now we’re confronted with turbulence and instability in the financial markets, so it’s of the utmost importance that we preserve Europe as a safe haven in this context,” she said.

Calvino, who heads the Luxembourg-based institution that is effectively the lending arm of the European Union, was speaking as euro-area finance ministers meet in Brussels for the first time since nominations closed for candidates to replace European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde.

See also: BMW widens battery component suppliers with Samsung, LG Energy

She expects her successor to “continue her policies and approach,” she said. “It is critical we preserve independence in decision making” at the ECB, she added.

Dutchman Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos are the two official candidates to succeed Lagarde, who is stepping down almost nine months early. Calvino described both as “very strong technically.”

Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting, Kyriakos Pierrakakis, president of the Eurogroup, said that the gathering would be an “information point” in the process of selecting a candidate.

See also: Alphabet mulls Asia bond sale as AI fears fuel global volatility — Bloomberg

“We understand that we need to move fast,” he said. “The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year. It’s a tight schedule.”

title: BMW widens battery component suppliers with Samsung, LG Energy
article:
(Nov 9): BMW AG is adding South Korean battery-cell makers Samsung SDI Co and LG Energy Solution Ltd to its supplier networks in Europe and the US, as the German carmaker looks to reduce dependencies.

Samsung will supply cells to BMW facilities in Europe while LG will provide them to plants in the US starting in the late 2020s, BMW said Monday. In Europe, BMW also uses cells from China’s CATL and EVE Energy Co.

The new partnerships come as BMW is scaling up production globally of its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries. The parts are central to its new generation of electric models such as the iX3 sport utility vehicle. The company is accelerating the phase-out of its older battery models, it said last week.

Along with a facility in China, the manufacturer has built up assembly plants for its latest batteries in Germany, Hungary, Mexico and South Carolina. It’s pushing to reduce distances between its suppliers that feed cells into those sites, and where it makes cars, it said.

The decision underscores how European and US carmakers are pushing to curtail their reliance on key components out of China. The country dominates global battery production and the processing of key materials, leaving carmakers exposed on capacity closer to their plants in Europe and North America.

Separately, the European Union is working on new regulation to encourage more local manufacturing. The rules as part of the Industrial Accelerator Act target certain thresholds where a majority of a vehicle must be made in the bloc to qualify for a range of subsidies.

See also: Alphabet mulls Asia bond sale as AI fears fuel global volatility — Bloomberg

title: Vietnam turns to taxes, state borrowing to finance growth push
article:
(Nov 9): Vietnam plans to step up tax collection and state borrowing next year, reducing its reliance on banks to finance a major infrastructure drive that’s key to its bid for double-digit economic growth.

The National Assembly on Monday approved a resolution setting the 2027 budget deficit at 739.6 trillion dong (US$28.9 billion), equivalent to 4.5% of gross domestic product (GDP), according to the government website. That’s higher than a target of 4.2% of GDP for this year.

Parliament aims to increase 2027 state revenue by 9.1% from this year, while calling on the government to intensify efforts to combat transfer pricing and tax evasion, and to recover outstanding tax debts, according to the post. The government is also tasked with broadening the tax base, particularly by strengthening collection from e-commerce, digital platform-based businesses, and mining.

Vietnam is diversifying its funding sources as ambitious growth targets and a sweeping infrastructure campaign stretch a banking system that already plays an outsized role in financing the economy. The nation is targeting at least 10% economic growth, but officials have warned of significant challenges, including mounting inflationary pressures and increasing demand for capital and energy.

Higher revenue targets could increase pressure on small businesses and households, with higher tax liabilities, compliance costs and more intensive enforcement potentially undermining private-sector growth and consumption. About 56,300 businesses closed in the first ten months of the year, more than double the number in the same period last year, according to state media.

A Vietnam Chamber of Commerce survey of 1,001 household businesses conducted in April found that tax compliance remains a top concern: 93% cited difficulties with tax procedures, 92% pointed to accounting requirements and a similar number expressed concern about higher taxes and fees this year.

See also: Asia’s innovation capacity is improving but could be better

State borrowing is also projected to increase by around 30% next year to 1,280 trillion dong, according to a separate parliamentary document, which does not elaborate on the sources of borrowing.

The Finance Ministry has been in talks with international banks about a potential sovereign dollar bond sale of up to US$1 billion. That would be the first such offering since 2014, though officials have been discussing the issuance for months without setting out a timeframe.

The higher deficit and borrowing targets underscore the need to increase state revenue while balancing government support to boost businesses. Finance Minister Ngo Van Tuan has estimated tax exemption and reduction policies in 2026 will total about 240 trillion dong, while tax payment extensions are expected to be around 120 trillion dong, according to the ministry’s news website.

title: Nvidia shares drop after CEO Huang’s affair triggers board probe
article:
(Nov 9): Nvidia Corp shares dropped after the company’s board launched an investigation into chief executive officer Jensen Huang, following his admission of an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy.

The stock was down about 3.7% on Robinhood’s trading platform Sunday night New York time. The revelation threatens Friday’s tentative rebound in the bellwether artificial intelligence chipmaker following a steep selloff on concerns over financing for Big Tech spending and the impact of US midterm elections.

The new crisis started over the weekend, after Huang admitted in an internal staff memo that he was unfaithful to his wife and apologsed to employees, prompting the firm’s board of directors to act. Their probe follows reports that Nvidia’s leader had been targeted by former Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying for China by US intelligence agencies.

President Donald Trump called the Nvidia CEO a “fine person,” and said he should stay on as leader of the chipmaker. Nvidia’s board said it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or the company’s secrets were compromised.

Nvidia’s stock is down about 22% from its October high. The internal inquiry casts a rare cloud of leadership uncertainty over the company, just days before it’s scheduled to report quarterly earnings on Nov 17.

See also: Anthropic buys power for AI data centres in US$3.4 bil deal, FT says

While Nvidia’s core business is expected to remain strong, analysts warned that any distraction at the top could create an overhang for the stock that has been the anchor of the global AI trades.

title: Alphabet mulls Asia bond sale as AI fears fuel global volatility — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 9): Alphabet Inc has had talks recently about potentially offering Hong Kong and Singapore dollar bonds, people familiar with the matter said, a deal that would test investor appetite in Asia after an AI selloff in global markets.

The Google parent had spoken with banks and investors about a debt sale as early as this month, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters. The company is looking to raise the equivalent of US$1 billion to US$1.5 billion in Hong Kong dollars and around US$1.5 billion in Singapore dollars, the people said. Proceeds would be used for general corporate purposes, they added.

Discussions are ongoing and details could still change, the people said.

The potential sale comes as investors worry about increased scrutiny of AI-related projects after Democratic gains in the US midterm elections. Credit spreads for some technology issuers have widened, hastening a repricing already underway in the global debt market, where a borrowing binge fueled by the AI boom has pushed up yields.

Alphabet said it doesn’t comment on market speculation, in response to a request for comment.

If successful, Alphabet’s bond offering would add to a busy year of debt issuance by the company. It has already tapped multiple markets, despite the growing investor concerns over the enormous capital commitments being made by technology companies to AI infrastructure.

See also: UniCredit profit at record as Orcel eyes Commerzbank control

Alphabet is among a group of hyperscalers, including Microsoft Corp, Amazon.com Inc and Meta Platforms Inc, that have borrowed at a record pace while simultaneously committing tens of billions of dollars to build out AI capabilities.

Just last week, Alphabet raised €6 billion (US$6.7 billion) through a multi-tranche euro bond sale, its second offering in the currency this year. The company paid materially higher borrowing costs than in its inaugural euro deal in May as concerns over the pace of AI spending rose.

The company has diversified its funding sources this year with transactions in other international markets, including an inaugural Australian dollar bond sale in August. It has also sold bonds in Swiss francs, British pounds, Canadian dollars and Japanese yen in 2026.

title: Credit Agricole proposes merging local unit with Banco BPM
article:
(Nov 9): Credit Agricole SA is seeking to merge its Italian operations with Banco BPM SpA, extending a wave of deals washing over the country’s finance industry.

The French bank has proposed to Banco BPM “to engage in discussions concerning a merger” between the Italian lender and Credit Agricole’s Italian unit, it said in a statement Monday.

“For the shareholders of Banco BPM, the proposal provides for an exchange ratio that reflects a 20% premium, in addition to the payment of an extraordinary dividend” of €1 billion to Banco BPM’s current shareholders, it said.

As a result of the proposed deal, Credit Agricole would increase from its current 29.6% stake in Banco BPM to approximately 45% of the new entity, it said. The transaction would be conditional on approval by Banco BPM’s shareholders and on exempting Credit Agricole from the obligation to launch a mandatory tender offer.

Banco BPM had a market capitalisation of about €20 billion (US$22 billion) at Friday’s close.

Credit Agricole is Banco BPM’s largest shareholder and it previously opposed an acquisition offer for the Italian bank from rival Monte Paschi.

See also: Mitsui Chemicals to take over chip linchpin JSR for US$12 bil

The French lender has previously indicated it’s in favour of a tie-up between its local operations and Banco BPM.

The expected synergies are estimated at €800 million per year.

title: UniCredit profit at record as Orcel eyes Commerzbank control
article:
(Nov 9): UniCredit SpA reported record quarterly profit as it lifted full year guidance, giving chief executive officer Andrea Orcel a tailwind as he nears control of Commerzbank AG.

Net income in the period increased 24% to €3.26 billion (US$3.6 billion) in the third quarter, the bank said in a statement Monday. That was higher than all estimates.

UniCredit also upgraded its full-year profit guidance before extraordinary charges to “well above” €11.5 billion from more than €11 billion and increased the planned interim dividend to €4.5 billion.

The Italian lender has won European Central Bank approval to raise its stake in Commerzbank above 30% and potentially to as much as 100% after a two-year pursuit that has met resistance in Germany.

UniCredit expects the outstanding regulatory processes to be completed late November, after which it would control close to 50% of Commerzbank’s voting rights. That would effectively give UniCredit control at shareholder meetings and allow Orcel to steer key decisions at the German lender.

The Milan-based bank said in the statement that new governance arrangements and the kick-off of “Commerzbank Unlocked” strategy are expected to be announced by the first quarter.

See also: China newspaper dismisses Jensen Huang spy claim, warns on ties

Orcel has indicated he intends to replace large parts of Commerzbank’s supervisory board and subsequently its top management, including chief executive officer Bettina Orlopp. The executive has also outlined thousands of potential job cuts and a substantial reduction in Commerzbank’s international offices.

Last week, the Frankfurt-based bank lowered its full-year outlook for income from lending amid intensifying competition for deposits. Orlopp struck a more conciliatory tone towards UniCredit during the earnings presentation, saying the two banks could work together on procurement, overlaps in their international networks and shared product platforms to generate savings and support revenue growth.

Germany, which owns about 13% of Commerzbank, is seeking commitments on jobs, lending to small and medium-sized companies, the bank’s Frankfurt headquarters and the preservation of its stock-market listing.

See also: Citadel Securities plots Asia push with hiring, office expansion

UniCredit also said that a combination with HypoVereinsbank, its existing German unit known as HVB, could unlock “substantial additional value and potentially earlier than expected.”

UniCredit profit was driven by higher revenue and lower costs.

“We have fundamentally transformed the way UniCredit operates, combining sustainable profitable growth with structural cost efficiency, disciplined capital allocation and a strong balance sheet,” Orcel said.

Revenue in the third quarter rose 12% from a year earlier, helped by higher income from lending, fees and dividends, while costs declined more than 1%.

The bank’s CET1 ratio rose to 15% at the end of September.

title: China newspaper dismisses Jensen Huang spy claim, warns on ties
article:
(Nov 9): A Chinese state-run newspaper denied Beijing had any link to Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair, accusing American media outlets of spreading a fabricated spy narrative and warning the issue could hurt ties.

The Global Times, a nationalist tabloid, said American outlets, in particular the New York Times, were “going crazy” with speculative stories.

“All it took were a few photographs showing Asian faces and Nvidia’s previous efforts to push for relaxing trade curbs on China,” the commentary said. “This is precisely how American media, which have long styled themselves as ‘objective,’ manufacture stories.”

“Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, someone often fires a cold shot from behind,” the newspaper said, claiming there were likely behind-the-scenes efforts to “stir up confrontation,” without providing any evidence. It warned that an “anti-China script” would disrupt normal tech and trade exchanges, and damage the interests of both sides.

Huang has admitted an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy. Last week, key House Republicans requested a briefing with Huang to discuss his dealings with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. To investigate the case, the Nvidia board is assembling a committee of independent directors who will work with outside counsel, according to a statement Sunday.

On Oct 30, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said a New York Times report that Huang was the target of a spy plot was “unsubstantiated”. “It is nothing but smears against China,” Guo said at the time.

See also: Citadel Securities plots Asia push with hiring, office expansion

US President Donald Trump is set to visit China next week for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where he will have his third sit-down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this year. The meeting will be closely watched for signs the leaders can sustain a fragile trade truce, especially after Trump’s Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections.

The Global Times commentary also compared the Huang episode with an incident in 2023 in which a Chinese balloon flew over the US, causing a diplomatic dispute. Beijing said a civilian airship used mainly for meteorological research strayed off course due to the weather, while Washington described it as a surveillance aircraft and shot it down over the sea.

title: China extends pause on 24% US tariffs to January, keeps 10% rate
article:
(Nov 9): China will suspend an additional 24% tariff on US goods for another two months, formalising a decision by the two countries’ leaders to prolong their trade truce until next January.

The move will take effect at 1:01pm Beijing time on Tuesday, with a 10% blanket tariff retained on US imports, the Customs Tariff Commission of the State Council said in a statement. China will also extend its suspension of special fees on American ships docking at its ports until Jan. 10, the Transport Ministry said in a separate statement on Monday.

The new timeline is a result of the agreement reached by Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in September to extend their tariff ceasefire until early next year. The truce, originally set to expire on Nov 10, was struck in Busan, South Korea in October 2025, where both sides agreed to suspend their mutual 24% levies while leaving the 10% rate in place.

The US and China imposed the levies at the start of their tit-for-tat trade escalation started by Trump shortly after he returned to the White House last year.

China said it will closely monitor US plans to replace Trump’s emergency tariffs — which were overturned by the Supreme Court earlier this year — with duties imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. In the statement, it warned that Beijing may adjust its countermeasures accordingly.

Trump and Xi are set to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen later this month for what will be their third summit this year. At their last round of talks in Washington in September, they agreed to extend the trade truce until Jan 10.

See also: China starts marketing green bonds for debut sales in Canada — Bloomberg

While US-China ties have stabilised, signs of tensions have lingered.

Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer spoke with China’s Vice Premier He Lifeng, raising concerns about Beijing’s recent actions and the importance of implementing commitments made as part of the deal reached in Busan.

In a statement, Greer’s office said he used a video call to emphasise the critical importance for China to take “concrete actions” to implement its pledges, specifically on “agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals.”

title: Citadel Securities plots Asia push with hiring, office expansion
article:
(Nov 9): Citadel Securities is plotting further growth of its trading business in Asia, adding more people and office space in what has become its second-largest revenue driver outside of the US.

The market maker is looking to partner with local and global banks to do more trading in Asia Pacific, according to chief executive Officer Peng Zhao. It’s increasing its office space in Hong Kong by 40%, adding half a floor at Two International Finance Centre.

“As we continue to grow our client business outside the US, there’s going to be increasing demand to trade non-US products and readiness on our side,” Zhao said in an interview from the firm’s Hong Kong office.

In recent years, Citadel Securities has been ramping up its presence in Asia as a non-bank market maker. It launched a structured-product business based in Hong Kong, buttressing its key business of matching buyers and sellers across the world in the US equity and fixed-income markets. Now, the firm is looking to go a step further.

Citadel Securities added nearly 100 people in Asia this year to bring its total headcount in the region to about 400. Almost half of this year’s hires are based in Hong Kong, with others working out of offices in Singapore, Sydney and Tokyo, Zhao said. Competition has been intensifying as peer Jane Street is growing its footprint in Hong Kong alongside other quant-driven funds.

“The talent base here in Asia is transforming from one that is largely technical to one that’s a healthy mix of technical talent as well as sales and trading,” Zhao said.

See also: Philippine economic slump worsens on Iran war, bad weather

Citadel Securities, which employs more than 1,800 people, has been making high-profile hires from banks and hedge funds to bolster its business that serves institutional investors in Asia. It tapped former Millennium India chief executive officer Prakash Subramanian KV as country head of India and Singapore, and Richard Smerin as global head of structured products from Morgan Stanley.

The firm officially launched its so-called high-touch equity trading this year to handle large orders of US stocks for institutional investors. Zhao says Citadel Securities saw the number of active clients double from the first half to the second half of the year. Those orders usually come directly from clients, and frequently require human intervention to keep costs down and minimise market impact.

In Asia markets, including Hong Kong, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, if the firm was to launch a similar, block-size trading offering for institutional investors it wouldn’t follow the same business model, according to Zhao. “I would expect more partnerships with local and global banks here in Asia,” he said.

See also: Lula vows fiscal responsibility in first address since election

“The combination of size of the market, market structure and client demand is going to dictate how we prioritise” plans moving forward, he said.

title: China starts marketing green bonds for debut sales in Canada — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 9): China is marketing green bonds in Canada for the first time, expanding its offshore debt footprint to finance sustainable projects as ties between the two nations warm.

The Ministry of Finance is starting to sell the yuan-denominated green sovereign bonds on Monday, with the initial price guidance for the three- and five-year notes at yields of around 1.8% and 1.9%, according to people familiar with the matter. The notes may be priced later Monday, they said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters. Royal Bank of Canada is a joint bookrunner for the sale, they added.

The sale follows the ministry’s announcement for plans to market up to four billion yuan (US$600 million) of green sovereign bonds in Canada this week. It would mark the ministry’s first offshore issuance of yuan-denominated bond beyond Hong Kong, Macau and London, Bloomberg-compiled data shows.

The yuan bond offering extends China’s push to promote currency internationalisation and connect with more overseas investors amid growing doubts over the dollar. This also coincides with improving bilateral relations between China and Canada, which includes an agreement last week to extend a tariff deal and continue discussions on boosting Canadian exports to the Asian nation.

The ministry did not explain the reasoning behind issuing a Hong Kong-listed bond in Canada. Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng is visiting Canada this week to co-chair the second China-Canada Economic and Financial Strategic Dialogue.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also plans to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month in China.

See also: China raises delegate count to 2,360 for 2027 party congress

In recent years, China has stepped up offshore green sovereign debt to showcase its commitment to a sustainable transition. The most recent issuance of such yuan green debt took place in May in Hong Kong, featuring three- and five-year notes priced at 1.42% and 1.56%, respectively.

title: Philippine economic slump worsens on Iran war, bad weather
article:
(Nov 9): The Philippine economy unexpectedly slowed for a fifth straight quarter, raising questions about the central bank’s rate-hike cycle and heaping pressure on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 2.1% in the three months to September from a year earlier, the statistics agency said Monday. That compares to 2.4% in the second quarter and was a full percentage point below the median estimate of 3.1% in a Bloomberg News survey.

Agricultural output fell 4.8% in the third quarter, and services growth continued to slow. Farm output was hurt as typhoons battered the climate-vulnerable nation, with El Niño further clouding the outlook.

The peso fell 0.3% and the benchmark stock index dropped as much as 0.7% after the data release, which underscores how deeply the nation is underperforming neighbouring economies. Growth was less than half the pace seen in Indonesia or Malaysia, and less than a quarter that of Vietnam.

The data underscore the damage to the Philippines from the US-Iran war, which has driven up crude oil prices and inflation, forcing the central bank to hike interest rates. The resulting higher cost of living and still-unresolved government corruption scandals have weakened consumer and business confidence.

High food and energy prices constrained consumer spending, a key economic driver which continued to post slower growth. Tighter financial conditions weighed on investments which remained in contraction. Cyclones and the monsoon disrupted farm production, which reduced rural incomes and added to supply pressures.

See also: Lula vows fiscal responsibility in first address since election

The data come days after the release of the latest inflation print showing an acceleration to 7.8% in October, the fastest pace in almost four years. That was expected to lead the central bank to continue raising rates following a jumbo 50-basis-point hike in October.

Economic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan refrained from calling on the Bangko ng Sentral Pilipinas (BSP) to pause its rate hikes, noting the central bank is trying to cool price gains.

“If the BSP actually succeeds in anchoring the inflation expectation back to the target, then that actually will impact positively consumption and investments,” he said at a briefing in Manila. “It’s not necessarily bad for growth.”

See also: UBS CEO Ermotti says midterms create uncertainty for AI buildout

Still, he said achieving the 2026 growth target of 3.5% to 4.5% is “very challenging at this point given the current environment but we are hoping that the fourth-quarter performance will be better.”

The BSP now must weigh the weak economy against surging prices and support for the peso, which has dropped almost 7% to be Asia’s second-worst-performing currency this year. Inflation has remained well above the central bank’s 3% goal since March.

“While we think they should still deliver more jumbo hikes, they may opt for a smaller hike in December because of growth concerns,” said Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. A small hike could leave the peso under greater pressure, he added.

“This could also increase the possibility of inflation getting de-anchored,” Neri said. “Core inflation is just rising too fast.”

Marcos will also face pressure to act to support the economy, which is heavily dependent on imported energy from the Middle East.

Growth started to slow in the third quarter of last year. At that time, confidence began a lengthy slump after Marcos revealed corruption in government involving billions of pesos in flood-related infrastructure. The graft scandal is unresolved, while Vice President Sara Duterte, who denies wrongdoing, is on trial in the Senate over alleged unexplained wealth.

title: Mitsui Chemicals to take over chip linchpin JSR for US$12 bil
article:
(Nov 9): Japan’s Mitsui Chemicals Inc is buying JSR Corp for ¥1.84 trillion (US$12 billion) with support from state-backed Development Bank of Japan (DBJ) to strengthen its hold over a key chip materials linchpin.

Mitsui Chemicals and DBJ will acquire all shares of JSR from government-backed Japan Investment Corp, the companies said in a filing Monday. DBJ will pay ¥200 billion in cash for a stake that will be converted to preferred shares without voting rights, it said.

The deal for JSR, one of the world’s leading makers of photoresists needed to make advanced chips, would further a government-backed effort to consolidate Japan’s fragmented semiconductor-materials industry. Japan is home to the world’s largest suppliers of silicon wafers and dominates several other critical chip materials, but many of its smaller suppliers remain vulnerable to foreign takeovers.

Mitsui Chemicals’ shares extended their decline to as much as 15% in Tokyo.

JIC took JSR private two years ago. JSR supplies light-sensitive materials used with ASML Holding NV’s extreme ultraviolet lithography machines to pattern fine circuits onto silicon wafers. Customers for JSR’s array of specialty chemicals include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, Intel Corp and Samsung Electronics Co, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Bloomberg News reported in September that JSR was weighing buyout proposals from Mitsui Chemicals and rival Mitsubishi Chemical Group Corp.

title: Lula vows fiscal responsibility in first address since election
article:
(Nov 9): President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pledged to preserve Brazil’s public finances without abandoning social programmes in his first televised address since winning a fourth term, as he sought to reassure investors.

“The trajectory of public debt and high interest rates concern me, which is why I reaffirm my commitment to fiscal responsibility, in order to make sustainable social policies possible and enable the much-needed expansion of investment,” Lula said in his Sunday remarks. “All of this will be done while preserving the fiscal rules.”

He cited lowering interest rates as one of the main challenges ahead, saying his government will create the conditions to reduce borrowing costs and help raise investment in the country to more than 20% of GDP.

The president, however, offered no details on spending cuts, revenue measures or other steps his administration could take to shore up the public accounts, a key concern for investors as he prepares for another four years in office.

The message marks an early attempt by the leftist leader to balance competing pressures: preserving the social agenda that has defined his political career while convincing investors his government can keep public finances under control and create conditions for interest rates to fall.

Brazilian assets have come under heavy pressure since Lula’s surprise runoff victory, amid market concerns that his fiscal approach will exacerbate budgetary strains and further complicate the central bank’s efforts to tamp down inflation.

See also: UBS CEO Ermotti says midterms create uncertainty for AI buildout

In his public address, Lula highlighted some of his government’s key achievements, including the passage of a shorter workweek. He also pledged to expand a series of government programs, including measures aimed at supporting small businesses.Lula, who was reelected on Oct. 25, used the roughly 8-minute address to thank Brazilians for giving him another term, with particular mention of young people, women and the elderly. He also sought to strike a conciliatory tone after a deeply divisive campaign, pledging to govern for all Brazilians and work to normalize political relations in the country.

“I am immensely grateful for the more than 64 million votes I received, and I will govern for all Brazilian women and men, as I have always done. We must build bridges instead of walls,” he said.

The 81-year-old leader, now entering his fourth term as Brazil’s president, faces a slowing economy and a growing number of families grappling with debt. In his speech, Lula highlighted a series of measures aimed at easing the financial burden on Brazilian households, including an income-tax exemption for those earning up to 5,000 reais (US$907) a month and a ban on online gambling.

See also: RBA’s Hunter says AI boom will put near-term pressure on CPI

“Without spending money on bets, families have increased consumption, retailers are selling more, industry is producing more and the wheels of the economy are turning again,” he said. “Betting destroyed lives and must remain in the past, like a nightmare from which Brazil has finally awakened.”

title: UBS CEO Ermotti says midterms create uncertainty for AI buildout
article:
(Nov 9): UBS Group AG chief executive officer Sergio Ermotti said the sweep of Democrats in the US midterm elections could trigger a slowdown in the construction of artificial intelligence capacity.

“Investors are rightly questioning the plausibility of how much value can be created out of this cycle,” he said in a Bloomberg Television interview in Sydney on Monday. “The problem being more on the timing, on how quickly can you really deliver all these benefits, and in that sense, you see a little bit of questioning around valuations that is important.”

Candidates who favor stricter oversight of AI won in key congressional races. The developments threaten an already-fragile backdrop for global markets as investors weigh valuations following declines in richly valued tech stocks.

“The political developments in the US may also trigger a slowdown in building up capacity,” Ermotti said. The AI cycle is “definitely going to be a very strong engine of growth, medium to long term. In the short term, it may still be a volatile topic, and that would create potential volatility in financial markets.”

The midterm elections have added a fresh catalyst to the unwinding of the AI trade, which had for weeks faced doubts over whether massive investments in the technology will pay off. Expectations for tighter regulation under a Democratic-controlled Congress are adding to concerns about the growth outlook for chipmakers and data center suppliers, helping drive the steepest decline in US tech stocks since 2020.Ermotti also said inflation remains a key risk that markets are struggling to price. Strong jobs data last week revived expectations for another interest-rate hike from the Federal Reserve.

It is “probably still underestimated how sticky inflation is, and the fact that central banks may need to keep rates higher for longer than expected,” he said.

See also: RBA’s Hunter says AI boom will put near-term pressure on CPI

Ermotti also said he wanted to see more appetite from policymakers in Europe to address concerns over fiscal conditions. Asked whether he was worried about stability of the financial system there following a surge in bond yields in France, Ermotti explained his concern.

“Worried is probably a little bit too far, but I’m concerned that things are not going to be taken seriously enough and fast enough in order to address the risk of contagion, which is probably the most significant one,” he said. “And in that sense, I do hope that the system will come up with urgent measures to contain that potential contagion.”

title: RBA’s Hunter says AI boom will put near-term pressure on CPI
article:
(Nov 9): A senior official at Australia’s central bank said surging investment in areas related to artificial intelligence will further fuel demand in the economy, at a time when policymakers are already aggressively raising interest rates to combat inflation.

In a speech on the potential impact of AI, Reserve Bank assistant governor Sarah Hunter on Monday called it among “the most significant technological developments of our time,” one already beginning to reshape the economy.

“In the near term, the positive shock to aggregate demand set against the economy’s current supply capacity will put some upward pressure on inflation,” she said. “Some liaison contacts are reporting that data centre construction is adding to demand for some already-stretched construction skilled trades.”

Rising construction costs are one channel AI demand is feeding through to the consumer price index, Hunter said during a Q&A after her speech. To a lesser extent, price rises for newer mobile phones and game consoles are also boosting the CPI, she added.

Australia’s construction project pipeline reached a record A$1.4 trillion through September and may end up double the scale of the mining boom, according to Deloitte Access Economics. Both the RBA and government have pointed out the surprising strength of business investment, even as the US-Iran war has pushed energy prices higher and weighed on households.

See also: Nvidia CEO’s affair engulfs AI giant in Chinese spying probe

Still, risks to the AI project pipeline are “balanced,” Hunter said in response to a question, pointing out that potential changes to regulation could crimp some developments.

The RBA has raised interest rates five times this year to 4.85%, an 18-year high, as it struggles to regain control over inflation.

On the upside, once initial bottlenecks are overcome, AI is expected to boost productivity because economies will be able to produce more with the same inputs. That suggests the initial inflationary pressures will dissipate in time, Hunter said in her speech, while acknowledging high uncertainty over the scale of gains.

See also: Australia home sales rise in fledgling sign of property recovery

“Current estimates for the impact of AI on annual productivity growth over the next decade range from over 2% to just 0.1%,” she said.

While Hunter said AI is likely to change the labour market significantly in time, to date it has been fairly muted.

“Contacts in the RBA’s liaison program indicate that AI has not yet impacted most firms’ headcount and is not expected to over the next year,” Hunter said.

“However, there are tentative signs of adjustment, through weaker job ad posting and employment outcomes in more AI-exposed occupations, and stronger growth in areas where the technology has had less of an impact, particularly for younger workers,” she said.

Global financial markets were whipsawed last week after the Democratic Party’s sweep of Congress in the US midterm elections, which stoked fear among investors about tighter regulation of the data center industry.

Hunter said the exposure of financial market participants to the AI investment boom is increasing at a time when investors are demanding very little compensation for taking on risky assets.

“If the returns to AI investment disappoint, some asset prices, including equities and corporate debt, will be exposed to sharp repricing and possibly disorderly adjustments,” she said.

title: Nvidia CEO’s affair engulfs AI giant in Chinese spying probe
article:
(Nov 9): In a 257-word memo to employees, Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang left no doubt that the chip colossus was embroiled in a crisis like none before in its three-decade history.

After months of reports about the CEO’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Huang admitted on Sunday that he’d had an affair and said the Nvidia board was launching an investigation. Huang had previously said there was nothing inappropriate about his relationship with the woman, who worked for a Singapore-based customer.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang, 63, said in the memo. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The stunning admission intensified the controversy surrounding a company at the heart of the artificial intelligence market — a sector that’s already been rocked by concerns about a slowdown in data centre spending. Nvidia makes chips that are crucial to AI computing equipment, and it’s one of the world’s most valuable companies.

Huang himself has been the AI field’s biggest cheerleader, drawing throngs of fans in what’s been called “Jensanity.” Wearing his signature leather jackets, he crisscrosses the globe to help promote the technology’s adoption — a shift he bills as a new industrial revolution. Nvidia also has emerged as a key source of financing for AI infrastructure. He has worked with some of Wall Street’s biggest firms on a US$500 billion effort to help companies rapidly build out their equipment, and he’s funnelled money into bolstering the AI supply chain and fledgling customers.

Though Huang will remain Nvidia CEO pending the results of the investigation, the incident marks a dramatic comedown for an AI evangelist at an already delicate moment.

See also: Australia home sales rise in fledgling sign of property recovery

“It is hard not to read the news over the weekend as negative given it brings the stewardship of one of America’s most important companies, and the architect of the US AI trajectory, under debate, as well as calling judgment into account,” Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said in a note.

President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday, calling him a “fine person” and saying he should remain CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it,” Trump told reporters. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”

See also: Thai spyware alerts prompt opposition leaders to demand probe

To investigate the case, the Nvidia board is assembling a committee of independent directors, who will work with outside counsel, according to a statement Sunday. A perpetual futures contract on the Hyperliquid blockchain referencing Nvidia’s share price fell about 2.9% in the wake of the announcement.

The probe follows a series of reports that Nvidia’s leader was targeted by former Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, who the US government suspects was recruited by a Chinese spy agency. The CEO previously said he had a “normal” business relationship with the woman, who is no longer at Megaspeed.

The board investigation will address reports that the chip magnate “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

In his memo, Huang said he will support the investigation. “I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security,” he said.

Nvidia’s co-founder — a leader famous for his hands-on and tireless management style — built the maker of graphics cards into arguably the world’s most important technology company. Nvidia’s highly prized accelerator chips are used to develop and run AI models, and Nvidia has branched out into related fields, including computers, networking and software.

Huang also has been a leading voice trying to calm fears about AI technology slipping out of human control. He has dismissed the need for the AI labs to slow down their work to ensure it doesn’t threaten humanity — even at a time when industry leaders such as Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have endorsed such an idea. He’s also argued that new regulations are unnecessary.

The Santa Clara, California-based company has no public succession plan, and there is no obvious heir apparent for Huang. He has repeatedly said he wants to continue in his role for decades and has created an informal organizational structure around him that eschews a conventional hierarchy. Instead, his direct reports are tasked with rapidly implementing his decisions.

Huang has said that this system gives his company the flexibility to react to rapid changes in technology and remain agile. But it’s also created a situation where there’s no replacement ready to step in and take over Huang’s relentless schedule.

The latest revelations “highlight the considerable key man risk that Nvidia faces,” Rasgon said. “Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia, clearly sets the long term strategy and direction, and (with supposedly 60 direct reports) pulls most of the company’s strings himself.”

Concerns that sensitive information might leak via Nvidia’s contacts with China have fueled calls for investigations and greater scrutiny of Huang and the company, ratcheting pressure in what has already been a difficult geopolitical balancing act. While Nvidia is allowed to ship a limited range of products to China under a licensing program granted by the current Trump administration, Beijing has restricted imports of the chips — an impasse that continues to curb the chipmaker’s sales in the world’s second-largest economy.

Huang has long sought to sell more of Nvidia’s AI processors in China, the largest market for chips. He’s argued that Nvidia and its peers should be allowed to serve the region to keep their products central to the development of AI. Closing off the market will risk turning China into a more powerful, independent force in artificial intelligence, he has said.

Investors have poured money into Nvidia, which reports earnings later this month, betting it will continue to be the main beneficiary of runaway spending on AI infrastructure.

The company reached a record market capitalization of nearly US$5.8 trillion in October. That has slipped below US$5 trillion, however, weighed down by concern about the sustainability of AI infrastructure build-out.

Megaspeed, based in Singapore, has been accused of breaking US export restrictions and smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang had told Bloomberg that his contacts with Megaspeed employees were typical of business relationships he has with many Chinese customers and executives.

title: Futures explained: What they are, how they work and where they may fit in an investor’s toolkit
article:
Investors today enjoy wider access to the global market and new trading technology. However, the understanding level of futures trading has not necessarily been able to keep pace.

So, what is a futures contract? It is a standardised agreement to either buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date. Contracts traded on regulated exchanges are centrally cleared and hence a clearing house, rather than the broker, stands between buyer and seller.

Traditionally, professional market participants employ futures trading for price discovery, hedging and obtaining market exposure, but retail investors often see this as a high-risk speculation.

Global futures trading reached 30.64 billion contracts in 2025, up 8.6% on 2024, and in the first eight months of 2026, futures volume ran 26.9% ahead of the same period last year, according to the Futures Industry Association (FIA).

When asked about some of the practical applications of futures trading for retail investors, Ken Ong, CEO of KGI Securities (Singapore) shares that one of them will be in the form of protection for their portfolio.

“Retail investors who own a portfolio of United States (US) stocks can use equity index futures to reduce exposure ahead of an event such as a Federal Reserve decision, without selling holdings they intend to keep for the long term,” Ong explains.

He believes that futures trading could also provide diversification to retail investors as the derivatives could give investors an efficient access to interest rates, energy, metals and agriculture, which are hard for individuals to reach directly.

“These matters more today than it have in many years, as the traditional relationship between stocks and bonds has proved less dependable as a hedge,” Ong elaborates.

Futures trading also allows investors to act on a macro conviction, long or short, with precise position sizing. “Investor behaviour already reflects this: CME Group's metals volume rose 34% to a record in 2025, with record trading in Micro Gold and Micro Silver futures,” Ong shares.

On the benefits of futures trading, it all boils down to how the futures market itself is structured in the first place, according to him.

“Futures are standardised, exchange-traded, central cleared and every participant sees the same price, and your broker is not the other side of your trade,” Ong elaborates.

Aside from standardisation, the depth and accessibility of the futures market brings about liquidity for retail investors. “CME Group averaged a record 28.1 million contracts a day in 2025, and its major markets trade almost around the clock on weekdays, which suits investors in Singapore's time zone,” Ong says.

Ong also highlights the benefit of a right-sized participation for retail investors in futures trading.

“Last December, Micro E-mini equity index futures and options accounted for 40.5% of all equity index volume at CME Group. This shows that smaller contracts are no longer a niche and have evolved into a mainstream way,” he adds.

He feels with this right-sizing feature, retail investors could see futures trading as a professional instrument with position sizes that aligns with their balance sheet.

While investors could see the benefits and practical application of futures trading, misconceptions tend to be one of the key areas that needs to be addressed as well, especially in futures trading.

“While futures are perceived as speculative tools, the futures market, however, exists primarily to manage risk, and some of the world's most conservative institutions are among its largest users,” Ong states.

Meanwhile, some retail investors might mistakenly believe that both contract for differences (CFD) and a futures contract are the same, but they are not.

“With a CFD, you hold a private contract with your provider while with a futures contract, you trade on a regulated exchange, and a central clearing house guarantees the trade,” he explains.

From his perspective, one of the misconceptions that is most worth correcting is that retail investors think that margin is a fee or that you cannot lose more than your deposit.

“Margin is likened to a good-faith deposit, and because leverage amplifies gains and losses alike, losses can exceed it. Investors who understand this from the start tend to trade far more responsibly,” Ong comments.

While accessibility for retail investors has been largely resolved through micro contracts and digital platforms, he sees the real bottleneck now to be competence and confidence within retail investors.

According to a 2025 survey conducted by the Securities Investors Association (Singapore) and Beansprout, they found that key barriers for beginner investors include a lack of familiarity and a lack of expert guidance.

“Hence, we need to allow investor’s education to be built into the trading experience rather than kept separate from it. We should also open up trading simulation as an on-ramp for them. Recently, CME Group has reported strong growth in new traders using simulated environments to begin their futures journey, and we see the same appetite here,” Ong elaborates.

He adds that having transparency and suitability checks at onboarding will allow retail investors to better understand various aspects of futures trading such as margin, leverage and costs before their first live trade.

“For me, I see this as a shared responsibility across exchanges, brokers and regulators. “Participation that grows without understanding is not sustainable, and our aim is to grow both together,” Ong believes.

For Ong, he would ask retail investors the following four questions before they commence their first futures trading.

“First, what is this trade for? Hedging, diversifying and speculating call for very different position sizes and time horizons. Second, do you understand the contract and the various terms such as contract size, tick value, margin requirement, trading hours and expiry. Together, these determine what every price move is worth to you.”

“Third, what will be the maximum loss? Leverage means losses can exceed your initial deposit, so decide your exit before you enter, use stop orders, and commit only capital you can afford to lose. Lastly, who is your counter party in this trade? Check that your broker is regulated, that you are trading genuine exchange-traded futures, and that costs are transparent,” Ong shares.

Retail investors should practice in a simulated account before committing real capital. “Investors who take that seriously are the ones best placed to benefit,” he adds.

Meanwhile, he shares that futures trading is not new at KGI Securities. “Our Singapore futures business traces back to Ong First Tradition, the country's first futures brokerage and a pioneer clearing member of SGX's derivatives market, established in 1984,” Ong reiterates.

“Today, KGI is a securities and derivatives trading and clearing member of SGX, and we provide futures execution and clearing to institutional and professional traders worldwide. We are now bringing that expertise to retail investors through a platform built specifically for them,” Ong reveals.

From his perspective, futures trading offered by KGI Securities opened up to a new generation of investors, and Ong believes that it will be better to develop it as a dedicated proposition than treat it as an afterthought.
